Cleaning Columns

Source: vignettes/cleaning_columns.Rmd
cleaning_columns.Rmd

Overview

Datasets rarely come with cleaned, tidy formatting in their column names and hence it is common practice to rename the original column names to those that are more code-friendly (i.e. lower-case, no spaces or special characters and unique). Alongside the code-friendly renamed columns, it’s also very practical to store label attributes, which act as a human-readable version of each column that can be used for displaying in tables and figures. Whilst there already exists functions for renaming columns (e.g. dplyr::rename()) and applying labels (e.g. labelled or Hmisc), there is much leg work that needs to be applied in setting up the inputs for these functions.

This vignette demonstrates how to use column dictionaries to expedite the process of standardising and labelling columns in a dataset. We will use two main functions from thekidsbiostats:

  • make_column_dict() – create a copy-pasteable column dictionary template.
  • update_columns() – rename and label columns using a column dictionary.
library(thekidsbiostats)


1. Create a data dictionary template: make_column_dict()

Suppose we use patients_raw from thekidsbiostats pacakge as an example:

data("patients_raw")

patients_raw |> dplyr::slice_head(n=10) |> gt::gt()
Patient ID Site Name trt_grp randomisation date AGE_yrs Sex Height (cm) WEIGHT_kg Do you smoke any form of tabacco product? Diabetes (Y/N) Cholesterol-Total eGFR HR_bpm SBP_baseline_mmHg DBP Baseline (mmHg) sbp.wk12 DBP_Week12
BP-001 Sydney Control 2025-08-26 55 Female 162.7 82.0 Former N 5.7 70 64 159 96 158 98
BP-002 Melbourne 5 mg/day 2025-03-14 76 Male 164.4 94.0 Never N 5.7 55 76 157 91 145 87
BP-003 Perth Control 2025-08-19 54 Female 163.9 75.9 Never N 4.0 93 59 153 97 153 96
BP-004 Perth Control 2025-03-14 52 Female 158.8 78.8 Never N 5.2 74 79 143 93 132 92
BP-005 Melbourne 10 mg/day 2025-02-28 57 Male 170.9 90.7 Never Y 5.9 90 59 148 84 131 86
BP-006 Perth Control 2025-02-24 75 Female 169.1 76.8 Never Y 5.4 57 76 150 86 149 82
BP-007 Melbourne 5 mg/day 2025-02-08 49 Female 164.3 59.4 Never N 5.0 78 71 137 86 125 78
BP-008 Brisbane 10 mg/day 2025-06-24 66 Female 173.6 78.1 Current N 5.0 82 73 141 88 132 85
BP-009 Perth Control 2025-04-06 52 Male 159.5 75.5 Never N 4.3 71 89 157 93 157 94
BP-010 Melbourne Control 2025-07-30 55 Female 161.0 76.8 Former Y 4.9 84 71 160 105 142 104


Beyond these names being inconsistent (mixed case, underscores, dots and spaces), they can also be tricky to reference when attempting to use them in coding operations. For example, let’s try to calculate the BMI of the patients.

patients_raw <- patients_raw |> 
  mutate(bmi = WEIGHT_kg / (`Height (cm)` / 100.0)^2)

head(patients_raw$bmi)
#> [1] 30.97696 34.77957 28.25426 31.24822 31.05440 26.85802

The spaces, question marks and parentheses in the column names require us to use backticks (` `) to avoid R interpreting these symbols literally. Functions such as janitor::clean_names() can be very useful for standardising such column with syntactic names. However, for situations like the column "Do you smoke any form of tabacco product?", the “cleaned” version (do_you_smoke_any_form_of_tabacco_product) is arguably just as unwieldy.

Nonetheless, the consequence of renaming columns for easy manipulation in code is that we will likely also drop potentially useful formatting stored in the columns (e.g. units and symbols). Ideally, we want the best of both worlds: clean column names and simultaneously retaining human-readable labels for presentation.


The solution is to manually set up a dictionary that maps the old column names to newly formatted column names as well as apply $label attributes to each column to be used for all visual presentation.

The make_column_dict() function makes this process easier by creating a ready-to-fill template based on the column names that exist within the data. For example:

dict <- make_column_dict(patients_raw, quiet=FALSE)  # note: setting auto_clean=FALSE will stop the janitor::clean_names() from being performed.
#> dict_patients_raw <- tribble(
#>   ~old, ~new, ~label,
#>   "Patient ID", "patient_id", "",
#>   "Site Name", "site_name", "",
#>   "trt_grp", "trt_grp", "",
#>   "randomisation date", "randomisation_date", "",
#>   "AGE_yrs", "age_yrs", "",
#>   "Sex", "sex", "",
#>   "Height (cm)", "height_cm", "",
#>   "WEIGHT_kg", "weight_kg", "",
#>   "Do you smoke any form of tabacco product?", "do_you_smoke_any_form_of_tabacco_product", "",
#>   "Diabetes (Y/N)", "diabetes_y_n", "",
#>   "Cholesterol-Total", "cholesterol_total", "",
#>   "eGFR", "e_gfr", "",
#>   "HR_bpm", "hr_bpm", "",
#>   "SBP_baseline_mmHg", "sbp_baseline_mm_hg", "",
#>   "DBP Baseline (mmHg)", "dbp_baseline_mm_hg", "",
#>   "sbp.wk12", "sbp_wk12", "",
#>   "DBP_Week12", "dbp_week12", "",
#>   "bmi", "bmi", "",
#> )

We can either directly modify the dict object assigned above or copy-paste the printed output into our code and modify as needed. Here we fill in the new names with cleaned, syntactic names and add a human-readable label for each column:

dict_patients <- tribble(
  ~old, ~new, ~label,
  'Patient ID', 'patient_id', 'Patient ID',
  'Site Name', 'site', 'Site name',
  'trt_grp', 'treatment', 'Treatment group',
  'randomisation date', 'rand_date', 'Randomisation date',
  'AGE_yrs', 'age', 'Age (years)',
  'Sex', 'sex', 'Sex',
  'Height (cm)', 'height_cm', 'Height (cm)',
  'WEIGHT_kg', 'weight_kg', 'Weight (kg)',
  'Do you smoke any form of tabacco product?', 'smoking_status', 'Smoking status',
  'Diabetes (Y/N)', 'diabetes', 'Diabetes (Y/N)',
  'Cholesterol-Total', 'chol_total', 'Total cholesterol (mmol/L)',
  'eGFR', 'egfr', 'eGFR',
  'HR_bpm', 'heart_rate', 'Heart rate (bpm)',
  'SBP_baseline_mmHg', 'sbp_baseline', 'Systolic BP baseline (mmHg)',
  'DBP Baseline (mmHg)', 'dbp_baseline', 'Diastolic BP baseline (mmHg)',
  'sbp.wk12', 'sbp_week12', 'Systolic BP week 12 (mmHg)',
  'DBP_Week12', 'dbp_week12', 'Diastolic BP week 12 (mmHg)',
)



2. Apply column dictionary: update_columns()

Now after having defined the column dictionary above, we can simply use the update_columns() function to apply these changes in a single line.

patients_clean <- update_columns(patients_raw, dict = dict_patients)
patients_clean |> dplyr::slice_head(n=10) |> gt::gt()
Patient ID Site name Treatment group Randomisation date Age (years) Sex Height (cm) Weight (kg) Smoking status Diabetes (Y/N) Total cholesterol (mmol/L) eGFR Heart rate (bpm) Systolic BP baseline (mmHg) Diastolic BP baseline (mmHg) Systolic BP week 12 (mmHg) Diastolic BP week 12 (mmHg) bmi

Writing/Loading column dictionaries from file

Both of these helper functions can accept file paths as input or output for the column dictionary. This is handled slightly differently for each:

  • make_column_dict(): the file argument accepts a character string defining the file path to write the dictionary to. The extensions ‘.csv’, ‘.txt’, ‘.rds’ and ‘.xlsx’ are accepted.
  • update_columns(): providing a file path in the form of a character string to the dict argument will attempt to load the dictionary directly from the file. In addition, the old, new and label parameters can be used to explicitly specify the names of the relevant columns if they are named differently.
